title: Grant Proposals and Funding
answer: Drafting, agency compliance, budgets, finding collaborators and predicting success.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing material a researcher has already written, such as prior grant narratives, progress reports, methods sections, and published papers, as the starting point for a new funding application.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body places on a proposal before it will be accepted for review, including page limits, font and margin requirements, required sections, reference styles, and the specific templates some agencies mandate.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs cover the money a funder agrees to provide for a project and the rules that decide which expenses that money may pay for.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators for a grant proposal means identifying the people whose skills, data, or facilities fill the gaps in your own team, and whose involvement strengthens the case you will make to a funder.

children.name: Predicting Proposal Success
children.blurb: Predicting proposal success is the use of statistical and machine learning models to estimate how likely a grant application is to be funded, or how it will score in review, before or alongside the actual review.

sections.body: Grant proposals are the documents researchers write to ask a funder for money, and artificial intelligence is now used across the whole cycle of producing them. Language models draft narrative sections from a lab's earlier papers and progress reports, turning years of results into a coherent case for the next project. Other tools check a draft against a funder's formatting rules, flag missing sections, and help assemble budgets from institutional cost rates. Some groups also use models to scan funding databases and publication records for potential collaborators, and to estimate how a proposal might fare against past award patterns. The work is administrative and editorial rather than scientific, but it consumes a large share of a researcher's time, which is why it attracts automation.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Drafting is the most mature use, and it works best when the model is grounded in the applicant's own prior text rather than asked to invent a research plan. Formatting and compliance checking are largely solved as document parsing problems, since funder rules are explicit and machine readable, though agencies update them and tools lag behind. Budget work is partly solved: models can total costs and catch obvious disallowed items, but institutional rates, cost sharing and agency specific allowables still need a human grants officer. Finding collaborators is a search and matching problem that models handle reasonably well, with the usual caveat that a plausible match is not a working relationship. Predicting success is the weakest area, because award decisions depend on panel composition, funding cycles and review culture that are not in the text, and past outcomes are a biased sample. Nothing here replaces the judgement of the applicant or the signature of an authorised official.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run roughly in the order a proposal comes together. Drafting Proposals from Past Work is the starting point, covering how to reuse a lab's own papers and reports as source material instead of asking a model to generate a project from nothing. Funder Formatting and Compliance then takes that draft and fits it to a specific agency's rules, page limits and required sections. Budgets and Allowable Costs handles the numbers, including what a given funder will and will not pay for and where human review is still needed. Finding Collaborators turns outward, using publication and funding records to suggest partners and to check what a team is missing. Predicting Proposal Success closes the set by looking at what past award data can and cannot tell an applicant, and why those estimates should be read with caution. A reader new to the area would start with drafting, while someone already writing proposals would go straight to compliance or budgets.
